title: Contextual estimation of link information gain
summary: Scores each new document on a topic by the 'quantity of new information' it contains beyond documents the user has already seen, using an ML model over semantic feature vectors, then ranks or presents the new documents by that score. The claims are framed around an automated assistant and a user's own viewing history, so it describes per-user re-ranking, not proven corpus-wide web ranking. The general principle (reward what the other results don't already say) is what Google's own guidance asks for.
keyClaims: Claim 1: an information gain score 'based on a quantity of new information included in the given new document ... that differs from the information extracted from each document of the first set'.
Claim 2: rank the new documents by information gain score.
Claims 3-4: score produced by a machine learning model over semantic feature vectors of the seen and new documents.
evidenceNote: Mechanism = speculative (one patent, assistant context). Principle = confirmed by Google docs: helpful-content questions ask for 'original information', 'beyond the obvious', and warn against 'mainly summarizing what others have to say'; rater guidance defines Originality as information 'not already available on other websites'; leak analysis shows an OriginalContentScore attribute.
applies: Our roundups pick only products that at least 2 top-10 pages recommend (product-agent) and the live posts say so ('the pick most top review sites agree on', 'Consumer Reports, RTINGS, Wired ... all single out'). That makes the product set and the verdict nearly identical to what the searcher has already seen in the top 5, i.e. low information gain. brief-agent already asks for 3-5 ourGain points, but nothing checks they are absent from the top results or that they are analysis rather than a restated pain point.

ruleProposals.change: ourGain needs at least 3 entries of `type` 'analysis' (a comparison or calculation from verified specs, e.g. pints per day per 100 sq ft, load-to-weight ratio, fire-rating minutes vs interior cubic feet), 'decision' (a who-should-buy-which rule or chooser table no top result gives) or 'situation' (a pain point answered with a concrete fix). Each entry lists `absentFrom: [the 5 top-result URLs you opened]`; an entry found in 2+ of them is a commonPoint, not ourGain.

Never justify a pick by other publishers' picks. The first 150 words name no other review publisher (Wirecutter, Consumer Reports, RTINGS, Wired, CNET, Tom's Guide, Digital Camera World, etc.), and each product's reason cites a spec, a calculation or an owner-reported fact. Who else recommends it can appear once per post, in the 'How we picked' section only. QA warns when a listed publisher name appears in the first 150 words or more than 3 times in the body.

Keep the '2+ top-10 pages recommend it' rule for most picks, but allow 1 pick per roundup that no top-10 page lists when verified specs show it fills a gap the consensus misses (smallest, cheapest UL-rated, highest load under X lb), marked `consensus: false` with the reason.

title: Site quality score
summary: Computes a site quality score as a ratio: unique queries (or clicks) that refer to the site, i.e. queries containing the site's name/label or navigational to it, divided by all unique queries (or clicks) whose selected result is a page on the site. The score is then used as a term in the quality scores of every resource on the site. In plain terms: a site people search for by name, relative to how much generic traffic it receives, is treated as higher quality.
keyClaims: Claim 1: site quality score from 'a ratio of a numerator based on the first count [queries categorized as referring to the site] and a denominator based on the second count [queries followed by a click on a resource in the site]', with a threshold subtracted and/or the denominator raised to a power between 0 and 1.
Claims 2-4: a query refers to the site when it contains a site label, a term determined to refer to the site, or is navigational to it.
Claim 8: the ratio is used as a term in computing quality scores for resources in the site.
evidenceNote: Same inventor and concept as the studied Panda patent US8682892B1 (reference queries). Leak analysis documents a site-level siteAuthority attribute 'applied in Qstar'; the DOJ exhibit confirms a document quality signal Q* and that Google's ranking guide says site-wide signals contribute. The exact brand-query formula is not confirmed.
applies: Search Console shows zero branded queries for all 3 sites in the last 30 days (no 'rentersmarthome', 'best safe site', etc.), so the numerator is ~0. best-tripod.com and best-safe.com are exact-match-style domains, so 'best tripod'/'best safe' searches read as generic queries, not navigational ones, which makes brand demand harder to earn (Google's EMD system and a leaked EMD demotion attribute also reduce credit for such names). Nothing in our agents builds named-brand demand.

ruleProposals.change: Track branded queries (site name and spaced/unspaced variants) as a weekly KPI: count, impressions, clicks. Target: non-zero within 60 days.

Every white-hat mention we earn (resource pages, expert quotes, community answers) uses the brand name (RenterSmartHome / Best Tripod / Best Safe) plus the named tool (RenterSmartHome Score, Tripod Buying Checklist), not a keyword anchor, so people search for the brand.

Replace the anonymous 'Editorial Team' Organization byline with a real, named person who actually reviews the posts (bio, photo, sameAs links). Never a made-up name or AI headshot (Google calls fabricated creator profiles deception).

title: Ranking search results
summary: For each group of resources (e.g. a site, identified by Internet address) Google counts independent incoming links (links from sources that are not related to or duplicates of the target) and reference queries (past queries categorized as referring to that group). The ratio of independent links to reference queries becomes a group-specific modification factor that multiplies the initial score of every page in the group for any query. A site whose pages are searched for a lot but that few independent sites link to gets its pages scaled down.
keyClaims: Claim 1: a 'group-specific modification factor ... based on the count of independent links and the count of reference queries for the group', which 'modifies initial scores generated for resources in the group in response to received search queries'.
Claim 5: groups identified by Internet address.

Description: the initial factor 'is a ratio of a number of independent links counted for the particular group to the number of reference queries'; independent means the source is not likely related to or a duplicate of the target.
evidenceNote: Patent expired (fee related), so not proof of current use. Google's ranking guide confirms link analysis and PageRank are core and that site-wide signals exist; the DOJ exhibit says PageRank 'continues to be one of the factors that goes into the quality signals'; leak analysis lists homepagePagerankNs (homepage PageRank attached to every document) and siteAuthority.
applies: rentersmarthome.us (Ahrefs, 2026-10-18): DR 0, 53 referring domains, all spam .xyz and nofollow, 0 editorial links; best-tripod/best-safe have no known editorial links either. Any site-level factor built from independent links is therefore at its floor, which caps every page, especially on 'best X' head terms where the top 10 are DR 75-95 publishers. Links between our own 3 sites would not count as independent (same owner) and must not be used as a scheme.

ruleProposals.change: While a site has fewer than 10 independent editorial referring domains, a new keyword needs at least 2 top-10 results that are forums/Reddit/Quora or DR < 30 sites (from the saved Ahrefs SERP); 'best X' head terms whose whole top 10 is DR >= 60 are parked as `later` instead of queued. Still 'best X for Y' first (owner rule).

Set a measurable white-hat target: earn 3-5 independent editorial referring domains per site per month (resource-page inclusion for the free checklists, expert answers to journalists, original data posts others cite). No paid links, PBNs, exchanges, or cross-links between our own 3 sites for ranking.

title: Modifying search result ranking based on implicit user feedback
summary: For each query-document pair, a relevance measure is the share of clicks that became long views (e.g. long clicks / all clicks), with views weighted by viewing time, by query category and by user type, and that measure is fed to the ranking engine for future searches of the same query. Short clicks (the searcher came straight back) lower the measure.
keyClaims: Claim 1: a measure of relevance 'based on a first number in relation to a second number', the first being a subset of views following a click, the second all views following a click, provided to a ranking engine.
Claim 4: first number = total long clicks, second = total clicks for that query.
Claims 3, 5-9: views weighted by viewing duration (continuous or by time categories), adjusted per query category and user type.
evidenceNote: DOJ trial exhibit PXR0357 (Pandu Nayak): 'Navboost, a measure of how frequently users ... click on a particular document for a particular query', using 'most recent 13 months of data'. Leak analysis shows goodClicks, badClicks and lastLongestClicks attributes. Exact formula of this patent is not confirmed.
applies: Click signals need impressions on page 1-2. In the last 30 days our query rows show 325 impressions/1 click (rentersmarthome), 149/2 (best-tripod) and 67/1 (best-safe); almost all impressions sit at positions 21-50+, where nobody clicks, so these pages have no click history to be promoted by. Pages that already reach 1-10 for long-tail queries are where long clicks can be earned first. ROUTINE.md already asks for click-earning titles and a first screen that delivers the promise; what is missing is a check that the visitor does not need to go back to compare.

ruleProposals.change: Every roundup has a 'Which one should you get?' chooser right after the top picks: a 3-6 row table or list of 'If you ... → get X because <spec>' lines covering each pick, so the reader can decide without returning to Google. QA warns if a roundup has no chooser block in its first 30% of words.
Pick first the posts with queries at positions 4-15 and 5+ impressions in 7 days (closest to page-1 clicks), before posts at 20-50.

title: Scoring candidate answer passages
summary: For question queries, Google takes candidate answer passages from the top-ranked pages (passage units are sentences or table cells under headings) and scores each one on query-term match, answer-term match (terms that occur across many top-ranked pages, weighted by IDF), whether it contains an entity of the type the answer needs, plus query-independent features: the page's ranking score, reputation and site quality score, a penalty for passages that mix two sections, and a penalty for passages that begin with a discourse boundary term.
keyClaims: Claim 1: answer score from a query term match score and an answer term match score.
Claims 3-5: answer terms = terms in the top-ranked resources, weighted by how many of them use the term times IDF.
Claim 6: score reduced if no entity of the expected answer type is in the passage.
Claims 8-10: query-independent score uses the resource's ranking score, reputation and 'a site quality score of a site that hosts the resource'.
Claims 11-12: score reduced if the passage spans two sections or 'begins with a discourse boundary term'.
evidenceNote: Google confirms a passage ranking system that identifies sections of a page (ranking-systems guide). The specific scoring features are from this patent and family (US9959315B1, US10019513B1 in queue).
applies: ROUTINE.md already requires each H2 to open with a bold direct answer and the live posts do this well. Gaps: no rule that the answer sentence is self-contained (starts with the subject, not 'However/Also/It/This'), names the expected answer type (number with unit, model name, yes/no) and stays inside its own section; and claim 10 means passages from a low site-quality site still lose, which loops back to the authority reasons.

ruleProposals.change: The bold first sentence under each question-style H2/H3 is 15-45 words, self-contained, starts with the subject noun (never However, But, Also, And, So, This, That, These, It, They, Yes/No alone), repeats the heading's key term and contains the answer type the heading asks for (a number with unit, a model name, or an explicit yes/no plus reason). QA warns on any section whose first word is in that list.

For each outline H2 that is a question, record `answerType` (number+unit | model | yes/no | steps) and 3-5 `answerTerms` that most top-5 results use in their answer to it; the writer must use them in that section's first two sentences.

title: Ranking documents based on user behavior and/or feature data
filed: 2004-06-17 (application US10/869,057, priority same day); granted 2010-05-11; status Expired - Lifetime (adjusted expiration 2025-03-16). Continuations filed 2010-03-19 (US12/728,015), 2012-01-10 (US13/347,472), 2016-03-30 (US15/085,826).
summary: The 'reasonable surfer' patent. Instead of treating every link on a page as equally likely to be followed (classic random-surfer PageRank), Google trains a model on link features plus real user navigation data to predict the probability each link is clicked, and passes rank to the target in proportion to that probability. The description gives examples of links that are unlikely to be followed ('Terms of Service' links, banner ads, links unrelated to the document) and example learned rules: larger anchor font, links nearer the top of the document, and links whose source and target share a topical cluster get a higher click probability.
keyClaims: Claim 1: train 'a model that identifies a probability that a particular link, with particular feature data, will be selected by a user' from link/source/target feature data and user navigation data; compute 'a rank for a particular target document ... based on the probability associated with one or more of the ... links that point to' it.

Claim 6: link features include anchor font size, 'a position of the ... link within' the source document, position in a list, font color, number of words and actual words in the anchor text, 'commerciality of the anchor text', 'a context of words before or after the' link, the anchor's topical cluster, and whether the link stays on the same host or domain.
Claim 5: source-document features include the number of links on the page, words in headings and how well the source's topical cluster matches the link's.

Description: positions measured 'above or below the first screenful', 'in a footer, in a sidebar'; example rule 'links positioned closer to the top of a document have a higher probability of being selected than links positioned toward the bottom'.
evidenceNote: Confirmed part: Google says it 'uses links as a signal when determining the relevancy of pages', that anchor text and 'the words before and after links matter', and asks for internal links 'in context' (Link best practices). The leak confirms Google stores per-anchor quality data (sourceType: anchors from high/medium/low quality source pages, also 'an importance indicator of an anchor'). Not confirmed: that placement/click-probability weighting runs today. The patent family was continued three times (2010, 2012, 2016), which shows Google kept the claims alive; the original patent has expired, which says nothing about use.
applies: Gap check 2026-10-24 (all 3 repos, src/content/blog): incoming internal links to new posts are almost never contextual. finalize -> addBacklinks() runs before a post's pubDate (isLive=false), so it only adds the new post to other posts' `related` list (rendered as the 'Related guides' cards at the very bottom of the page, after the author box). data/ reports: rentersmarthome 150 related-box vs 2 contextual, best-tripod 107 vs 0, best-safe 86 vs 0; nothing converts them into body links once the post goes live (improve-agent adds 2-3 only for the one post it picks). Outgoing body links are also bottom-heavy: of body internal links, 104/228 (rsh), 98/178 (tripod), 67/115 (safe) sit in the last 20% of the body, and only 26/55, 10/38, 8/30 posts have any internal link in the first third. writer-agent's 'end with 1-2 links to the next question' rule reinforces this. Under the reasonable-surfer model these are the lowest-weight positions (bottom, card lists). Anchors are descriptive (no 'click here' found), but many are '<topic> guide' stubs ('pistol safe guide', 'HomeKit guide').

ruleProposals.change: When a post goes live (the hourly Scheduled release / go-live check), run the contextual backlink pass for it: insert 1 in-body link to the new post into each of 2 related LIVE English posts (pickLinkTargets score > 0.05), in a body paragraph (not a heading, list, table, FAQ or the related box), preferring the first half of the body; anchor = a natural 2-6 word phrase that names the new post's topic. Then run factcheck '<added one internal link to <slug>, no claim changed>' and qa for each edited post. Test: data reports show mode 'contextual' >= 2 for every post live 24h+.

Place at least 1 of the 3-5 internal links in running text within the first third of the body (intro or the first two H2 sections), where it answers a question the reader has at that point; keep the 1-2 next-question links at the end. Anchor text names the target page's topic in 2-6 words (e.g. 'fire ratings for gun safes', not 'gun safe guide'), never chained next to another link. QA warns when no /blog/ link appears in the first third of the body.

title: Predicting site quality
filed: 2013-03-15 (application US13/843,150, priority same day); published as US20140280011A1 2014-09-18; granted 2017-09-19; status Active (adjusted expiration 2035-08-24). EP and WO counterparts withdrawn/ceased.
summary: For a new site that has no baseline site quality score yet, Google predicts one from the site's text. It builds a phrase model from already-scored sites: for each n-gram (2- to 5-grams, tokenization not normalized, so errors are kept) it records on what share of a site's pages the phrase appears and the average quality score of sites with that share. A new site's predicted score is the central tendency of the scores of its phrases, weighted and smoothed toward a neutral score when a few very frequent phrases dominate. The predicted score is used as the site quality input when ranking the new site's pages. The description adds the model can also score 'a single page, paragraph, sentence'.
keyClaims: Claim 1: phrase model mapping 'phrase specific relative frequency measures' ('how many pages in a site contain the phrase relative to how many pages are on the respective site') to the average baseline quality score of previously scored sites; for a new site, the 'aggregate site quality score' is 'a measure of central tendency' of its phrases' scores; the predicted score is then used in 'generating respective ranking scores' for its pages.
Claim 2: phrases are 2-, 3-, 4- or 5-gram token sequences.

Description: phrases that are equally common on good and bad sites (example 'on the') are dropped as uninformative; if the top N phrases carry too much of the weight, the score is smoothed toward the neutral (global average) score; a minimum number of known phrases is needed before a prediction is made.
evidenceNote: Mechanism (n-gram phrase model) = speculative, one patent. Principle = confirmed by Google: the helpful content update 'introduces a new site-wide signal', the classifier is 'entirely automated, using a machine-learning model', it 'runs continuously, allowing it to monitor newly-launched sites', and 'Any content ... on sites determined to have relatively high amounts of unhelpful content overall is less likely to perform well'. Same inventor (Navneet Panda) as the studied Panda patents US8682892B1 and US9031929B1.
applies: All three sites are new (first impressions in October 2026), so a predicted, content-derived site score is exactly what they would get before any links or brand queries exist. Site-wide repeated wording is what such a model sees. Measured on src/content/blog (5-grams on >=30% of posts): the story block opener 'From our notes: When we lined up (the spec sheets / the listings)...' appears in 26/55 rentersmarthome, 29/38 best-tripod and 22/30 best-safe posts; nothing else repeats that widely in the markdown. The 'From our notes' label is an owner rule and stays; the identical opening sentence pattern is writer habit. Template blocks rendered by PostPage.astro ('How we picked these', 'Why you can trust this guide', affiliate disclosure) repeat on every page but are site design (boilerplate) and are not proposed for change. GSC: median position 43 (rsh), 26 (tripod), 54 (safe); 1-3 clicks per site in 30 days.

ruleProposals.change: Keep the '> **From our notes:**' label (owner rule), but the block's first sentence must be specific to this post (name the product, number or situation in the first 12 words) and must not reuse an opener already in another post: never start with 'When we lined up'. QA warns when the first 6 words after the label match the first 6 words of the story block in any other English post of the same repo.

Site-level repetition check: warn when any 6-word phrase in the new post's body (excluding product names, headings and the owner-mandated labels) already appears in 30%+ of the repo's English posts, and list the phrase so the writer can rephrase it. Test: the check flags 'from our notes when we lined' on today's corpus.
